prompt.context: Our client is an Australian mining company whose main product is gold, which it sells exclusively to China. This company is the largest producer by volume in the Chinese market with 200 tons sold each year. It is also the lowest-cost producer at $1,000 per ounce of production costs. Total Chinese demand for gold today is approximately 1,500 tons per year. The client has won a concession to mine a new site adjacent to its biggest mine, which would increase production to 300 tons per year (100 additional tons per year).
prompt.question: Is this expansion worth doing?

clarifying_info.q: Are there company criteria for approving projects?
clarifying_info.a: The board typically approves projects with a payback period of less than 5 years. Use undiscounted payback for any math.

clarifying_info.q: Where is the new mine located relative to existing operations?
clarifying_info.a: The new mine is adjacent to the original mine.

clarifying_info.q: How is the market expected to grow?
clarifying_info.a: The market will remain flat at 1,500 tons per year for the foreseeable future.

clarifying_info.q: How much upfront investment is required?
What are the production costs at the new mine? Are there cost synergies?
clarifying_info.a: Production cost is the same at $1,000 per ounce — no cost synergies.

clarifying_info.q: What does the competitive landscape look like?
clarifying_info.a: You can refer to Exhibit 1 (gold cost curve) once you are ready to dive in.

exhibits.title: China's Gold Cost Curve (includes royalties and freight)
exhibits.shows: A supply-cost curve for gold delivered to China. Each bar represents a supplier's cumulative volume (tons) on the x-axis and their cost per ounce (US$/oz) on the y-axis. Client A and Competitor B are labeled.

data.current_market_clearing_price: $1,200/oz (price set by marginal ton at 1,500 tons)

framework: Undiscounted Cash Flow analysis: incremental revenues minus incremental operating costs minus upfront investment
Incremental Revenue: assess how adding 100 tons affects commodity price (marginal-cost pricing shifts the market clearing price)
Direct Operating Costs: labor, repairs & maintenance, royalties, production taxes, freight (land and ocean), processing/cleaning, fuel, utilities
Indirect / Semi-variable Costs: synergies from shared overhead or additional overhead at scale
Upfront Investment: $750M capital requirement, evaluate against payback threshold
Risk Factors — Macro: China trade relations, GDP slowdown, competitor reaction, M&A activity, shipping cost shifts, mining/environmental regulation
Risk Factors — Operational: skilled labor supply, purchasing, distribution, royalty negotiation with Australia, safety stock for key machinery

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what happens to the gold price if the client adds 100 tons of supply to a 1,500-ton market?
questions.guidance: In a commodity market, price is set by the cost of the last (marginal) ton demanded. Currently total supply = 1,500 tons and the marginal ton costs $1,200/oz. Adding 100 tons shifts the supply curve right so the new marginal ton (ton 1,500) is now at $1,150/oz. The candidate should explicitly state this commodity pricing mechanic and identify that price falls from $1,200 to $1,150/oz.

questions.prompt: Calculate the payback period for the $750M investment.
questions.guidance: Candidate must use the oz-to-ton conversion (15 oz/lb, 2,000 lb/ton = 30,000 oz/ton), then compute profit before and after expansion, derive incremental annual profit, and divide investment by incremental profit.

math.setup: Conversion: 15 oz/lb x 2,000 lb/ton = 30,000 oz/ton. Before expansion: 200 tons at $1,200/oz price and $1,000/oz cost. After expansion: 300 tons at $1,150/oz price and $1,000/oz cost.
steps: Before annual profit = $200/oz x 30,000 oz/ton x 200 tons = $1,200M/year
After annual profit = $150/oz x 30,000 oz/ton x 300 tons = $1,350M/year
math.answer: 5-year payback period — exactly at the board's threshold.

brainstorming.prompt: If you were Competitor B, how would you react to this expansion?

categories.name: Capacity & Volume Response
ideas: Increase own production if access to new mines exists — volume gain may offset lower price, though further price pressure results
Temporarily reduce production to tighten supply and push prices back up

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Invest in operational efficiency to lower cost per ounce and protect margins at the new $1,150 price

categories.name: M&A / Consolidation
ideas: Acquire higher-cost producers that are struggling with the price drop, potentially realizing synergies
Consider merging with client or other mid-cost players to rationalize supply

categories.name: Strategic Context — Why Competitor B's Reaction Is Limited
ideas: Competitor B currently sells 200 tons at $1,025/oz cost; its margin drops from $175/oz to $125/oz, a $50/oz loss totaling ~$300M/year
To push the price below $1,150, Competitor B would need to add ~150 more tons (75% capacity increase) — a major and costly undertaking
Therefore, an aggressive volume response from Competitor B is unlikely in the near term

recommendation: Recommend the client proceed with the expansion
The $150M incremental annual profit delivers a 5-year payback, exactly meeting the board's threshold
Greater scale strengthens supplier bargaining power and provides flexibility to bring volume on or off the market advantageously
risks: Payback is right at the 5-year threshold — any cost overrun or demand softness makes the project NPV-negative
Price pressure could worsen if multiple competitors react simultaneously
Regulatory or royalty changes in Australia could compress margins
next_steps: Develop a skilled-labor attraction and retention strategy to address workforce supply risk at the new site
Conduct deeper due diligence on capital cost estimate ($750M) to ensure no overruns
Monitor competitor B and other mid-cost producers for capacity expansion signals
